clue.text: William in general service has an outlet for foul language here

parts.note: Bill is the short form of the name William
taken as written
G is a standard abbreviation for general
S is a standard abbreviation for service
a gate is a way out of an enclosure

explanation.surface: A soldier called William, serving in the forces, has a place where he can let rip with his swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: BILLINGSGATE was London's fish market, whose porters were famous for their coarse speech, so the name came to mean abusive talk; 'here' points at the market as the place it comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The market's porters swore so freely that its name became a byword for vulgar abuse.

clue.text: The sort of tack the best or worst of us take.

definitions.text: The sort of tack the best or worst of us take.

parts.words: The sort of tack the best or worst of us take
parts.note: hard tack is a dry ship's food, and the idiom 'takes the ...' is said of anyone who is outstandingly good or bad

explanation.surface: A remark about the approach people choose to take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tack' suggests a course or approach, but hard tack is sailors' dry ration. To 'take the biscuit' (British idiom) is to be the most extreme, at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard tack is a dry cracker eaten at sea, and the idiom about taking one praises or condemns the extreme.

clue.text: Left bird, right beast!

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless Australian bird

explanation.surface: A bird flew off left and an animal appeared on the right.
explanation.definitionFit: This primate from Madagascar is an animal.

clue.text: Oil rig mob 'mix-up'

indicators.note: mix-up signals that the letters of the three words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A brawl among the workers on an oil platform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mix-up' jumbles OIL RIG MOB and also defines the answer, so the whole clue does both jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A confused, embarrassing tangle of a situation.

clue.text: Kingdom of Landseer's stag

parts.note: Landseer's painting 'The Monarch of the ...' shows a stag ruling a Highland valley

explanation.surface: Asking which realm the painter's deer rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edwin Landseer's Victorian painting of a red deer stag is called 'The Monarch of the Glen', so the valley is its kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: The painted stag is called the monarch of a Scottish valley, so that valley is his realm.

clue.text: Golf club employee at the pub

definitions.meaning: a groundsman who looks after the greens on a golf course
a common English pub name, from the leafy figure of folklore

explanation.surface: A golf club worker having a drink at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The Green Man is a common English pub name.
explanation.definitionFit: A greenkeeper on a golf course, and the name of many English inns.

clue.text: Put it in the barn made for it

definitions.text: Put it in the barn made for it

indicators.note: in says one word goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Telling someone to store something in the barn built to hold it.
explanation.walkthrough: IT goes inside THE; the whole clue also describes the answer, since a tithe barn was built to store the tenth of produce owed to the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenth of farm produce paid to the church was stored in a special barn.

clue.text: Gold in a greenfly? Monsieur makes a witty saying

indicators.note: in says the word for gold is placed inside the insect

parts.note: an aphis is a greenfly
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A Frenchman makes a clever remark about gold inside a garden pest.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold; APHIS is the singular of aphids.
explanation.definitionFit: A pithy maxim that expresses a general truth.

clue.text: "Coton's full of nameless ——" (Brooke)

parts.note: a line from Rupert Brooke's poem 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester', mocking villages near Cambridge

explanation.surface: A quotation with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Brooke's poem mocks villages near Grantchester: 'And Barton men make Cockney rhymes, / And Coton's full of nameless ...'. Coton is a village west of Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme with 'rhymes' in Brooke's line is the word for offences against the law.

clue.text: Musically it isn't half long !

parts.note: in music a note named as half of the old 'breve' (literally 'short') is in fact the longest note in common use, so 'isn't half long' (British for 'is very long') fits it

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a piece of music goes on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: A breve was once the short note; the note called its half is now the longest note normally written, a whole note in American terms. 'Isn't half' is British slang for 'is very'.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole note, worth four crotchets, is named as half a breve yet is very long in modern notation.

clue.text: A trip perhaps in a zoo

definitions.text: A trip perhaps in a zoo

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the two words may be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: An outing that might be to the zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the letters of A TRIP; the whole clue then describes the animal, a hoofed snouted beast you might see at a zoo.
explanation.definitionFit: This hoofed mammal with a short trunk is a typical zoo animal.

clue.text: High class publicity man returning to fork out

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage, as in 'U and non-U'
a PRO is a public relations officer

indicators.note: returning says the little word to is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A posh press agent heading home to pay up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fork out' looks like 'pay', but here it means digging something out of the ground with a garden fork. U means upper class in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting a plant out with a garden fork pulls it up by the roots.

clue.text: Wait here — it may be a bit of a mess

definitions.meaning: a small waiting room off a larger room

definitions.text: it may be a bit of a mess
definitions.meaning: a military mess, where officers eat, often has a room attached as part of it

explanation.surface: Someone is told to wait in a room that is rather untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' suggests untidiness, but it is the dining hall of a military unit, and this room is part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A waiting room leading into a larger hall, such as the outer room of an officers' mess.

clue.text: Get to grips with gear

definitions.meaning: to ... a problem is to deal with it directly

explanation.surface: Someone sets to work on their kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the verb for confronting a task and the noun for equipment, as in fishing kit.

clue.text: Daddy Longlegs bids, bird begone

parts.note: the crane is a long-legged wading bird
fly here means go away quickly

explanation.surface: A long-legged insect tells a bird to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bids' links: the insect's name is an order to the bird to go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Daddy longlegs is the popular name for this long-legged insect.

clue.text: Airborne islands of song?

parts.note: songbirds that fly, named after the Atlantic island group where they come from

explanation.surface: An imagined archipelago floating in the air, full of music.
explanation.walkthrough: The birds take their name from the island group off north-west Africa, so a flock of them is a set of flying, singing islands.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow songbirds share their name with the Spanish islands they came from.

clue.text: Quality of a kind of square payment to Caesar

parts.note: a T-square is a drawing instrument
tribute was money paid to Rome

explanation.surface: The quality of a square deal in paying what is owed to Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: A characteristic or property belonging to something.

clue.text: Last bloody place for die-hards to die in Worcestershire

parts.note: red is the colour of blood
die-hards fight to the 'last ditch', the final line of defence

explanation.surface: A gory final stand where the diehards fall, set in Worcestershire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' points to the phrase 'last ditch', where die-hards fight to the end. Redditch is a town in Worcestershire, a county in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: A Midlands town in the county of Worcestershire, south of Birmingham.

clue.text: Briny-born Edward may well be salty

parts.note: the briny is an informal name for the sea
a son is one born to a parent
Ed is the short form of Edward

explanation.surface: A sailor called Edward, born at sea, would naturally be an old salt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salty' plays on the old sea dog: a weathered sailor is called seasoned, and salted food is seasoned too.
explanation.definitionFit: Food with salt added has been flavoured, and a salty old sailor is an experienced one.

clue.text: Poet breaks up a posh piano

indicators.note: breaks up says the letters are smashed and put together again

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A poet wrecks an expensive piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks up' jumbles A, POSH and P.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek lyric writer from Lesbos.

clue.text: A bad penny must unfortunately return

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
RE is short for return, as in the prefix re- meaning back

explanation.surface: The saying that a bad penny always turns up again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' shuffles MUST with RE, the short form taken from 'return'. The surface plays on the proverb that a bad penny always comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for a counterfeit coin or worthless cheque.

clue.text: Language of love ?

definitions.meaning: French, Italian and Spanish are tongues of this family, descended from Latin

explanation.surface: Asking which tongue suits a lover.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived language family, and a love affair.

clue.text: Prevent description, say, of crosswords made in advance

indicators.note: say marks that the description is a sound-alike of the word wanted

parts.note: crosswords whose clues were written beforehand could be called pre-clued

explanation.surface: Someone argues that preparing a description of the crosswords beforehand would stop something happening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'description ... of' frames the phrase; spoken, PRE-CLUED, clues written in advance, sounds like the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule something out in advance is to stop it happening.

clue.text: How to finish the curtains, say, with flax

indicators.note: say marks that the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: curtains are finished by giving them a lining, 'line 'em'

explanation.surface: Advice on finishing curtains using linen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'line 'em', said quickly, sounds like the botanical name for flax.
explanation.definitionFit: The botanical genus name of the flax plant.

clue.text: The Crown did without a measure for printers

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so did goes around the a

parts.note: taken as written
an em is a printer's unit of width

explanation.surface: The monarchy managed without a printing measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means outside, not lacking: DID goes around A.
explanation.definitionFit: A jewelled band worn on the head as a sign of royalty.

clue.text: Meaning of " leeway "

definitions.meaning: the general sense or gist of what is said
the sideways movement of a ship carried off course by wind

explanation.surface: Asking what the word 'leeway' means.
explanation.definitionFit: The gist of an argument, and a ship's sideways slide off course.

clue.text: Monotonous bit of scenery

definitions.meaning: a painted panel of stage scenery

explanation.surface: Some dull stage background.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull and lifeless in tone, and a painted canvas panel on a stage set.

clue.text: Capture of Paris

parts.note: in Greek legend the Trojan prince Paris carried off the Spartan queen, starting the Trojan War

explanation.surface: A city falls to an army.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris is the Trojan prince, not the French capital; his 'capture' is the woman he abducted from Sparta.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spartan queen was abducted by the Trojan prince, causing the war with Troy.

clue.text: William Bowman organizes a ruin of this planet

parts.note: William Tell, the Swiss archer of legend

indicators.note: organizes means the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A man named William Bowman tidies up a ruined building on Earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'William Bowman' looks like a name, but it is William Tell, the archer; 'organizes' rearranges A RUIN into URIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: From the Latin for earth, it describes anything belonging to our world.

clue.text: Some current success. "Issue of Fire", about the Colosseum

parts.note: an amp is a unit of electric current
a hit is a success
heat is what a fire gives off
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A newspaper item about the electric success of a fire-themed production at the Colosseum.
explanation.walkthrough: AMP, HIT, HEAT and RE are placed side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: The Colosseum in Rome is the most famous example of a Roman oval arena with tiered seating.
